title: Why Do I Need to Know This
author: Science of Learning
summary: When students ask why they need to learn foundational knowledge like multiplication tables, teachers should reframe the answer away from hypothetical real-world scenarios and toward cognitive science: foundational knowledge is not valuable for immediate utility but as a gateway concept that builds mental structures enabling future learning. New knowledge functions like a ratchet—once secured in long-term memory, it frees up working memory, reduces cognitive load, and enables increasingly complex thinking over time. Mathematics exemplifies this hierarchy: automaticity in basic operations supports fractions, ratios, proportional reasoning, and algebra; early gaps in foundational knowledge compound into later inaccessibility of advanced coursework and narrowed life opportunities.
points: Foundational knowledge teaches not because students will use it tomorrow but because it enables them to learn more powerful ideas later; schools build mental structures gradually, like constructing a multi-story building where early concrete work supports everything above.

Automaticity in basic operations frees working memory and facilitates learning of progressively complex concepts; math is relentlessly hierarchical, and early mastery gaps snowball into later inaccessibility and narrowed career options.

When students ask 'Why do I need to know this?' they often signal confusion, fatigue, or frustration, not philosophical disagreement about curriculum design; the real task is to diagnose missing prerequisite knowledge and design conditions for clarity and success.

Understanding itself creates meaning: students who can see, feel, and use their growing competence typically stop questioning why content matters; effort feels worthwhile when they experience accomplishment and realize their new capabilities.
quotes: New knowledge is like a ratchet: once knowledge and skills are securely stored in long-term memory, they don't just sit there—they make the next layer of learning possible. Each new concept builds on what came before, allowing students to handle ideas that would have been impossible or overwhelmingly difficult a few years earlier.

We teach the multiplication tables not because adults need to multiply numbers by hand, but because they are a gateway concept. Automaticity in basic operations frees up working memory, which in turn facilitates the learning of fractions, ratios, proportional reasoning, algebra, and much of higher mathematics.

Learning can be likened to the construction of a multi-storey building. For weeks, all that seems to happen is digging, pouring concrete, laying rebar, and checking measurements. To an outside observer—especially one who doesn't understand construction—it can look as though nothing useful is being built. But the crew is constructing the foundation that will support everything that comes later.

When students ask, 'Why do we need to know this?', they are often not asking a philosophical question about curriculum design. More often, it is a sign they are experiencing confusion, fatigue, or frustration. In those moments, a speech about relevance misses the point.

A student who understands what is going on is less likely to wonder why the content matters. When students experience clarity, progress, and competence, effort begins to feel worthwhile. They feel a sense of accomplishment and can appreciate their new understanding.” Archived from Science of Learning Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
